info.text: Susan Heitler's framework for conflict resolution therapy, which treats the strategies people use to end conflicts as the same small set whether the conflict is between two people or inside one. The five strategies -- fight, submit, flee, freeze, problem-solve -- are Pruitt and Rubin's; the claim that they run inward as well as outward is Heitler's own. The book dates from 1990 and its clinical categories reflect that; what has held up, and what this puzzle is built from, is the structural account.

clusters.name: Fighting
clusters.fact: Contending means trying to impose your preferred solution on the other party -- by insisting, blaming, criticizing, shouting, or force. Heitler's move is to notice that the same strategy runs inward with no second party required. Projection attacks in someone else what a person cannot bear to see in themselves; self-criticism attacks their own thoughts and feelings directly. The target changes. The strategy does not. Two people both contending produces arguments, and can escalate from there.

blaming.text: Assigning the problem to the other party: 'If you hadn't...' It settles the question of cause before anyone has looked into it.

criticizing.text: Attacking the person rather than naming what you want: 'Why did you have to...?!'

projection.text: Blame and criticism aimed at another person in place of seeing the same quality in oneself. Contending, with a substitute opponent.

self-criticism.text: Attacking one's own thoughts or feelings. The contending strategy turned inward, with both parties inside one person.

info.text: Trying to impose your preferred solution -- on the other party, or on the part of yourself that disagrees.

citations.title: From Conflict to Resolution: Rethinking Intimate Relationships and Family Therapy
citations.author: Susan Heitler

clusters.name: Yielding
clusters.fact: Yielding lowers your aspirations and settles for less than you would have liked. It ends the conflict immediately and at a cost that is invisible in the moment, because the person paying it is the only one who knows what was on the table. From outside it can look like generosity, flexibility, or an easy temperament, which is part of why it can run for years without anyone naming it.

denying own preferences.text: Ceasing to register what you want at all, rather than wanting it and conceding. The version that is hardest to notice from inside.

giving in.text: Agreeing to what the other party wants, often specifically to end the conflict rather than because you were persuaded.

lowering aspirations.text: Settling for less than you would have liked, and treating the reduced version as what you wanted.

info.text: Ending the conflict by lowering your own aspirations and settling for less than you wanted.

citations.title: From Conflict to Resolution: Rethinking Intimate Relationships and Family Therapy
citations.author: Susan Heitler

clusters.name: Fleeing
clusters.fact: Withdrawing leaves the scene of the conflict -- physically, by ceasing to talk, or by moving the conversation somewhere else. Turned inward it becomes leaving the scene of a thought: denial blocks an uncomfortable reality out of awareness, and obsessional thinking crowds it out with something absorbing and safe. Two people both fleeing produces a household where nothing is ever discussed and nobody can say what is wrong.

changing the topic.text: Leaving the conflict without leaving the room. Cheaper than walking out and harder to object to.

denial.text: Blocking an uncomfortable thought, feeling, or reality out of awareness entirely. Fleeing something you cannot physically walk away from.

leaving the scene.text: Departing the conflict physically, or cognitively and emotionally while still present.

obsessional thinking.text: Preoccupation with compelling but safe thoughts that crowd out frightening ones. Somewhere to go without moving.

info.text: Leaving the scene of the conflict -- the room, the conversation, or the thought.

citations.title: From Conflict to Resolution: Rethinking Intimate Relationships and Family Therapy
citations.author: Susan Heitler

clusters.name: Waiting
clusters.fact: Inaction waits for the other party's next move. It is the hardest of the four to recognise as a strategy, because from inside it feels like not doing anything -- which is exactly what it is, and exactly why it functions as an exit. Nothing is decided and nobody has to decide it. Two parties both waiting produces a negotiation that never concludes and a tension that never resolves.

passivity.text: Doing nothing in the hope that the situation will improve on its own.

procrastination.text: The everyday form: the thing that would settle it stays undone, and the not-doing is never quite a decision.

waiting for the other's move.text: Choosing to let the other party act first, which leaves the outcome to whoever tires of waiting.

info.text: Waiting for the other party's next move rather than making one.

citations.title: From Conflict to Resolution: Rethinking Intimate Relationships and Family Therapy
citations.author: Susan Heitler

clusters.name: Problem-solving
clusters.fact: Problem-solving pursues alternatives that satisfy both sides, and Heitler's components of it are all things you could check in a transcript: whether people say what they want, whether they take in what was said, whether airtime and volume run roughly even, and whether anyone ever states back what the two of them have arrived at. Notice what these have in common. Every one of them takes time -- which is the reason the other four keep winning.

receptive listening.text: Taking in what the other person said and building on it, rather than continuing your own train of thought or hunting for what is wrong in theirs.

saying what is wanted.text: Stating your own preference directly, rather than hinting at it, asking about theirs, or naming what you don't want.

summarizing statement.text: Saying back what the two of you have arrived at, including the part that came from the other person. Its absence is a red flag on its own.

symmetry.text: Roughly even airtime, volume, speaking rate, and turns in the speaking and listening roles. Asymmetry shows up in a recording before it shows up in anyone's account of the conversation.

info.text: Pursuing alternatives that satisfy both sides, and the observable components that make that possible.

citations.title: From Conflict to Resolution: Rethinking Intimate Relationships and Family Therapy
citations.author: Susan Heitler

bridges.fact: One party presses and the other stops naming what they want, largely to keep the first from turning critical. What makes this pattern durable is that it stops registering as a conflict at all: nobody is arguing. Heitler notes that the yielding partner may feel virtuous, martyred, resentful, or low, sometimes in rotation, and that none of those feelings point at the arrangement producing them.

info.text: The pattern where one party contends and the other yields, producing an arrangement that looks settled from outside.

bridges.fact: One party presses; the other declines to move. What comes out is nagging on one side and passive-aggressive response on the other, and each experiences the pattern as caused entirely by the other person. Neither is doing anything they would describe as the problem. They are each responding to a strategy, and it is the combination that locks.

info.text: The pattern where one party contends and the other waits, producing pressure met by delay.

bridges.fact: The reply beginning 'yes, but' has the form of listening and the function of contending. The acknowledgement in front is doing no work; everything after it is the message. This is why a transcript can show two people taking polite turns while nothing either of them says is being taken in by the other -- the machinery of dialogue running with the substance removed.

info.text: A response that concedes a token point and then advances one's own position anyway: 'Yes, but...'

bridges.fact: 'What do you want to do?' can be an invitation or an evasion, and the words do not tell you which. Asked instead of saying what you want, it hands the decision -- and the exposure that comes with wanting something -- to the other person, while presenting as the more considerate move. Heitler lists it among the ways people substitute for saying what they want.

info.text: Putting a question where a statement of one's own feeling or preference belongs.

lenses.prompt: Which of these can a person do entirely alone, with no second party involved?
lenses.explanation: This is Heitler's central move and the reason one book covers individual, couple and family therapy at once. Sorted by psychoanalytic lineage, projection and denial and obsessional thinking belong to a completely different literature than nagging and changing the subject. Sorted by what strategy they are, each is the inward version of something you can watch two people do. Waiting for the other's move is the excluded case and the distinction is exact: it needs someone whose move you are waiting for.

reasons.denial: Fleeing a reality you cannot walk away from.
reasons.obsessional thinking: Somewhere to go that requires no exit.
reasons.procrastination: The other party is the task, not a person.
reasons.projection: Contending, with the opponent supplied from inside.
reasons.self-criticism: Both parties to the fight are in one head.

lenses.prompt: Which of these stand in the place of saying what you actually want, rather than in the place of taking in what the other person said?
lenses.explanation: Heitler organises the warning signs by what they substitute for, which is more useful than a list of bad habits because it tells you what is missing rather than only what is present. Everything here stands in the place of saying what you want. The contradicting response is excluded and the contrast is worth holding: 'yes, but' is a failure to take in what the other person said, not a failure to state your own position -- the speaker's position is the one thing it makes perfectly clear.

reasons.asking instead of stating: A question where your own preference belongs.
reasons.blaming: States what the other party did wrong instead of what you want done.
reasons.criticizing: Names a fault in the person in place of a request.
reasons.denying own preferences: There is no want left to state.
reasons.giving in: Adopts their preference rather than putting yours forward.

lenses.prompt: Which of these could not happen at all without language?
lenses.explanation: Heitler's table has an animal column, and four of the five strategies have an entry in it: a cornered animal can fight, flee, freeze or submit, and does all four without a word. Problem-solve has a blank there, and this round is why. Three of its four components are made entirely of talk, and so are the contending moves that most resemble them. That is also why problem-solving is the slow option, and why the fast ones keep winning. Symmetry is the excluded case and it is the interesting one: airtime, volume and turn-taking can be measured in an exchange containing no words at all, which is why it is the component you could check from a recording in a language you do not speak.

reasons.blaming: Assigning cause is a claim, and a claim has to be stated.
reasons.contradicting response: Concede-then-advance is a sentence before it is a tactic.
reasons.criticizing: A verdict on a person has to be uttered to land as one.
reasons.receptive listening: Something has to have been said before it can be taken in.
reasons.summarizing statement: Stating back a shared position has no wordless form.

entries.reason: Heitler opens from negotiation theory and the prisoner's dilemma; see what the same escape problem looks like when the parties are strangers rather than intimates.
